name: Saint Vincent
rule: Plant Protection Act 16 of 2005 section 2 limits plants to living material and manufactured plant products to products whose nature or processing may create pest-introduction/spread risk. Sections 10(2) and 11 attach permits/certificates to specified covered articles rather than all plant-derived food. The manufactured-tea facts and ISPM32 Category 1 example supply a reasoned factual basis for applying the statutory boundary without a bespoke tea ruling. The regulated-article definition concerns material capable of carrying/spreading pests and deemed to require measures; clean new retail/postal packaging alone is not evidence of such a designation. The 2019 ministry notice applies to covered plant parts/products and is not read to erase section 2. The newly recovered official two-page commodity guidance names planting materials and specific fruits, roots, flowers and vegetables, not tea; it is undated and not treated as an exhaustive current waiver. Section 15 postal reporting and section 12 inspection remain ordinary controls and do not expand the defined commodity class.
personalMailApplicability: This conclusion follows commodity scope in the applicable local law, not a baggage, gift or noncommercial-seller exception. It applies to the stated private direct postal purchase and clean new packaging.
authority: St Vincent and the Grenadines Plant Protection and Quarantine
researchAttempts: Read the original Act PDF, including cover and section 1 confirming Act No. 16 of 2005, assented 25 October 2005. Corrected the previous 2015 citation. Section 2 defines plants as living plants, and manufactured plant products by potential pest risk; sections 10(2), 11 and 15 supply designation, permit and postal provisions.

Read the ministry’s AgriC Info September 2019, PDF page 14 (General Plant Quarantine Import Requirements), using OCR of the official PDF image. It requires permits for personal-use plant parts and plant products for processing/other purposes, with phytosanitary certification for the regulated consignment. It supplies no manufactured-tea or small personal-mail exception.

Rechecked the government-notified WTO import-licensing guidance and targeted official processed-food, tea and personal-import searches. No public commodity specification resolved whether finished sencha meets the Act’s manufactured-product risk threshold; kept unresolved rather than extending general plant guidance automatically.

2026-09-30: Read the official Licenses/Permits import guide, distinguishing its health-inspection requirement for imported food from origin veterinary certificates in the meat section. Retrieved the full text and reviewed the food, inspection, cargo-health and regulation-making provisions of the 1991 Environmental Health Services Act (Act 14/1991) from the National Parks government site; its food-handling and cargo-health powers do not establish a universal origin-law/free-sale certificate duty. Current consolidated Public Health Act 1977 food-import rules were not publicly recovered. Retained the exact Act 16/2005 agricultural classification gap rather than converting an inspection heading into a certificate obligation.

30 September bounded legal-scope peer review: Section 10(2) authorises controls for specified covered articles rather than itself listing all foods. Current ministry guidance includes personal-use plants/plant parts and plant products for processing or other purposes, but still does not define the risk status of finished manufactured tea. The 2019 list explicitly says it is not exhaustive. Section 13 release after inspection is not an advance permit/certificate waiver. No complete commodity exemption schedule is present in the Act.

2026-09-30 fresh official online recovery: Recovered the official import-agencies guide: plant conditions concern plant material; the origin health-certificate statement concerns meat, while general food undergoes inspection. No unqualified origin certificate for private tea established. Revisited Act 2005 sections5(a),10–11 with the actual current-linked ISPM 32 tea Category 1 illustration. NPPO duty to implement international standards and use standards in permit evaluation does not itself publish a local processed-tea commodity condition; retained unresolved. Saved vc-import-agencies.html.

30 September renewed general-definition review, superseding the earlier demand for a local tea-specific classification: Plant Protection Act 16 of 2005 section 2 limits plants to living material and manufactured plant products to products whose nature or processing may create pest-introduction/spread risk. Sections 10(2) and 11 attach permits/certificates to specified covered articles rather than all plant-derived food. The manufactured-tea facts and ISPM32 Category 1 example supply a reasoned factual basis for applying the statutory boundary without a bespoke tea ruling. The regulated-article definition concerns material capable of carrying/spreading pests and deemed to require measures; clean new retail/postal packaging alone is not evidence of such a designation. The 2019 ministry notice applies to covered plant parts/products and is not read to erase section 2. The newly recovered official two-page commodity guidance names planting materials and specific fruits, roots, flowers and vegetables, not tea; it is undated and not treated as an exhaustive current waiver. Section 15 postal reporting and section 12 inspection remain ordinary controls and do not expand the defined commodity class. The actual product is pure Camellia sinensis sencha manufactured by steaming to arrest enzyme activity, repeated rolling/pressing with hot air, and drying, then supplied sealed for infusion. MAFF describes this manufacture. ISPM32 section 2 and Appendix 2 identify manufactured tea as Category 1, supporting the factual conclusion that this differs from merely dried raw botanical material. The international standard is used as technical evidence when applying the local definition, not as an automatically binding local exemption. Ordinary inspection, food safety and pest freedom remain conditions; this is not a route for raw/sun-dried leaves, seeds, blends or contaminated goods.

requiredDocument: Ordinary postal/customs declaration and any ordinary arrival inspection; no special plant permit or phytosanitary certificate under this reasoned general-category interpretation.
definitionReview: Proposal for independent root review; not yet merged. See caribbean-finished-tea-definition-review/review-notes.json.
